description: Bukwus (Bakwas) is the wild man of the woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a small green spirit with a skeletal face and long curving nose. He prowls the deep forests, whistling to lure the living toward the realm of the dead; some accounts name him the husband of Dzunukwa, the Cannibal Woman, and his masked figure appears in the winter ceremonial.
source: Boas Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) ethnography; Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology; spiritsofthewestcoast.com
research_notes: Attested. Bukwus (Bakwas) is documented in Boas's Kwakiutl ethnography as king of the ghosts, a small green forest spirit with a skeletal face and long curving nose who lures the living toward the land of the dead; some versions make him Dzunukwa's husband. His masked figure appears in the winter ceremonial. Region is British Columbia, Canada (input says United States).

description: Baxbaxwalanuksiwe', the Man-Eater at the North End of the World, is the supreme cannibal spirit of the Kwakwaka'wakw and patron of the Hamatsa. Covered with mouths over his whole body, he commands the man-eating birds and possesses initiates of the winter ceremony; the northern lights are said to be the smoke of his far-off fireplace.
source: U'mista Cultural Society; Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology; Boas Kwakiutl texts
research_notes: Attested. Baxbaxwalanuksiwe' ('Man-Eater at the North End of the World') is the central spirit of the Kwakwaka'wakw Hamatsa ceremony, a being covered in mouths who transforms into the man-eating birds. The northern lights and rainbow are described as the smoke of his fireplace. Documented at U'mista Cultural Society and in Boas's Kwakiutl texts.

description: Boqs is the hairy wild man of the woods of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola), a giant sasquatch-like being of the British Columbia coast whose hands and face are human. He walks stooping, can raise the very land by supernatural power, and was said to still haunt King Island; Boas recorded detailed first-hand accounts.
source: Boas, The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians (1898); Suttles Bella Coola accounts (bigfootencounters.com)
research_notes: Attested. Boqs is the Nuxalk wild man of the woods, a sasquatch-like being with human hands and face who walks stooping and can raise the land by supernatural power; Boas recorded accounts of Bella Coola hunters near Namu and King Island. In the Bella Coola hero tale 'The Child and the Cannibal' the name labels a man-eating monster a magical boy defeats. Region: BC, Canada.

description: Blue Jay (Iqesqes) is the trickster hero of the Chinook and southern Salishan peoples, a bright-feathered being who is benevolent but hopelessly foolish. He blunders into the Land of the Dead with his sister Ioi and, through disrespect, brings disaster, and his tales of the spirit world are told as warnings and slapstick.
source: Boas, Chinook Texts (1894); native-languages.org Blue Jay
research_notes: Attested. Blue Jay (Iqesqes) is the Chinook trickster hero, also told by southern Salishan tribes; benevolent but extremely foolish. His best-known tale is the visit to the Land of the Dead with his sister Ioi, in which his disrespect causes disaster. Recorded in Boas's Chinook Texts (1894, BAE Bulletin 20) and summarized at native-languages.org.

description: Br'er Bear is a figure of African American folktale, one of the animal characters of the Uncle Remus cycle set down by Joel Chandler Harris from stories carried from West Africa. Slow-witted and gullible, he is strong but easily led, and both Br'er Rabbit and Br'er Fox trick him; he embodies brute strength without cunning.
source: Joel Chandler Harris, Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (1881)
research_notes: Attested, but not Native American. Br'er Bear belongs to African American folktale of the Uncle Remus cycle (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881), rooted in West African trickster stories. He is the strong, gullible adversary tricked by Br'er Rabbit. The input correctly lists the culture as African American; no Native attribution is implied.

description: Br'er Wolf is a figure of African American folktale from the Uncle Remus cycle compiled by Joel Chandler Harris, a hungry and determined predator who hunts Br'er Rabbit but is repeatedly outwitted. Persistent yet lacking cunning, he loses to the rabbit's tricks, reinforcing the theme that wit defeats strength.
source: Joel Chandler Harris, Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (1881)
research_notes: Attested, but not Native American. Br'er Wolf is an African American folktale figure of the Uncle Remus cycle (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881), drawn from West African trickster traditions. He persistently hunts Br'er Rabbit and is outwitted. Correctly filed under African American culture; not a Native figure.

description: The Sun is a powerful sky deity of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola), who dwells in a celestial house and carries the torches that light the day. He tests his sons-in-law with impossible tasks, and in the origin tale his mortal wife bears a son who takes the sun's course, burns the earth, and is cast down to become the mink.
source: Stith Thompson, Tales of the North American Indian (1929); native-languages.org 'The Man Who Acted as the Sun'
research_notes: Attested. The Nuxalk Sun is a sky deity of Bella Coola tradition who keeps the day's torches and tests suitors of his daughter. The tale 'The Man Who Acted as the Sun' (Stith Thompson, 1929) recounts the sun's son who, after being teased, carries the torches too early, scorches the earth, and is turned into the mink.

description: Tsilwalagame is the child of Dzunukwa, the Cannibal Woman of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, a boy found and adopted by a human ancestor. Though half of the wild cannibal people, he was raised among humans and became the ancestor of the 'Namgis; Mungo Martin's 1953 Thunderbird Park pole shows Dzunukwa holding him.
source: Royal BC Museum Thunderbird Park pole documentation; roadstories.ca; Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Tsilwalagame is the child of Dzunukwa in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition; in the origin story a human ancestor adopts him and he becomes ancestor of the 'Namgis/Nimpkish. Mungo Martin's 1953 Thunderbird Park pole (Royal BC Museum) depicts Dzunukwa holding her child. The input's 'child-stealing forest spirit' framing is imprecise.

description: Blue Jay is the trickster of Coast Salish and southern Salishan tradition, a clever but reckless bird-being whose adventures cross between the human and spirit worlds. Told by the Saanich and neighboring peoples, he is helpful yet foolish, and his brushes with the supernatural carry warnings about proper conduct.
source: native-languages.org Blue Jay; Coast Salish oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Blue Jay is the trickster of the Chinook and southern Salishan tribes, including Coast Salish peoples such as the Saanich. He is benevolent but extremely foolish, and his tales, including journeys to the spirit world, teach proper behavior. Documented at native-languages.org and in Coast Salish story collections.

description: Coyote is the trickster and culture hero of the Comanche, a figure of great power but little sense whose adventures shape the world. His stories, told as winter entertainment, recount both his cleverness and his greed, teaching lessons and explaining features of the natural world.
source: Comanche oral tradition; 'Coyote Tales of the Comanche' (World History Encyclopedia)
research_notes: Attested. Coyote is a central trickster and culture hero of the Comanche, a figure both clever and foolish whose tales teach lessons and explain natural features. Documented in 'Coyote Tales of the Comanche' (World History Encyclopedia, 2025) and Comanche oral tradition.

The name is associated with the Nuxalk origin account of Ista, the First Woman who descended to land, and with the creation of the first people; closer documentation is needed before the figure can be verified.

The name 'Patsallht' could not be independently verified in Nuxalk (Bella Coola) sources; it is connected in the input to the story of Ista, the First Woman who descended to land (smayusta origin account, nuxalk.net). Marked unattested pending better documentation; Ista and the Nuxalk origin narrative are the closest real analogues.

description: The Undersea Chief is the ruler of the ocean's wealth in the traditions of the Northwest Coast, master of salmon, halibut, and other sea creatures that sustain human life. While the Kwakwaka'wakw name him Komokwa and place him in a copper house beneath the sea, the Haida tell of their own masters of the undersea villages.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition; Wikipedia Kumugwe; Haida sea tradition
research_notes: Attested as a regional figure, with an attribution caveat. The undersea chief who owns the wealth of the sea is a shared Northwest Coast concept. The name Komokwa (Kumugwe) is Kwakwaka'wakw, not Haida; the input's story 'komokwa-and-the-undersea-kingdom-haida' blends the two. Description notes this so the Haida entry is not falsely credited with a Kwakwaka'wakw name.

description: Ts'uu Jaas, the Cedar Woman, is a spirit of Haida tradition who is bound to the cedar tree. Cedar gave the Haida their homes, canoes, clothing, and totem poles, and Cedar Woman is honored as 'every woman's sister,' a reminder that the people and the tree live together in a relationship of use and gratitude.
source: Haida oral tradition; K. Martin, Ts'uu Jaasgalang Hlgaajuu (UBC); Cedar Sisters framework
research_notes: Attested. Ts'uu Jaas (Cedar Woman) is a Haida spirit of the cedar tree, honored as 'every woman's sister'; cedar provided homes, canoes, clothing, and poles. Documented in Haida tradition and in UBC scholarship on cedar. The input's 'demonic-entity' archetype is wrong; she is a beneficent provider.

description: Yeil, the Raven, is the great trickster and creator of the Tlingit, who stole the sun, moon, and stars in nested boxes and released them into the sky. He shaped the landscape, brought salmon to the rivers, and gave fire to the people; his lineage, the Raven moiety, is one of the two primary divisions of Tlingit society.
source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909); Sealaska Heritage Institute; Dauenhauer, Adventures of Raven
research_notes: Attested. Yeil is the Tlingit Raven, the central trickster-creator who stole the sun and stars and shaped the world; the Raven moiety is one of two primary Tlingit kinship divisions. Documented in Swanton's Tlingit Myths and Texts and in Dauenhauer's Yéil Kundaayáyi (Adventures of Raven).

description: Robin is the long-suffering elder brother of Blue Jay in Chinook myth as recorded by Franz Boas. Patient and obedient, Robin endures Blue Jay's tantrums, sings at his shamanic cures, and helps gather the payments of roots, meat, and grease that the brothers bring home after healing the duck and the wolf girl.
source: Boas, Chinook Texts (1894), myth 13 'Robin and Blue-Jay'
research_notes: Attested. In Boas's Chinook Texts (1894, BAE Bulletin 20), myth 13 'Robin and Blue-Jay' makes Robin the elder brother of the trickster Blue Jay; he is patient and helps Blue Jay in his curing adventures. The input's claim that a story explains the robin's red breast was not confirmed in the tale itself.

description: The Magical Boy is the young hero of a Bella Coola (Nuxalk) legend, a child of humble birth who, aided by spirit power, confronts a man-eating monster that has terrorized the people. Where strength fails, his courage and cleverness prevail, and the tale stands as a hero-child story of the Nuxalk.
source: First People legends, 'The Child and the Cannibal' (Bella Coola); native-languages.org Nuxalk legends
research_notes: Attested. The Bella Coola (Nuxalk) legend 'The Child and the Cannibal' tells of a magical boy who defeats a man-eating monster; it is indexed in native-languages.org Nuxalk legends and retold at firstpeople.us. The hero-child theme matches the Nuxalk Boqs cycle.

description: Sinti Lapitta is the great horned serpent of Choctaw tradition, a giant water snake with two horns on its head, in some accounts a panther head, that lives in the deep waters. It possesses great power and wisdom and was said to visit unusually wise young men, granting them knowledge and strength.
source: Choctaw oral tradition; Akers, Choctaw mythology (2013); folklore.earth
research_notes: Attested. Sinti Lapitta is the Choctaw horned serpent, a water monster with horns (or a panther head) that grants power and wisdom to unusually wise young men. Documented in Akers' study of Choctaw mythology (2013) and in Choctaw oral tradition; related to the pan-Mississippian horned serpent.

description: The Masmasalanicw, the Four Carpenters, are the supernatural craftsmen of Nuxalk (Bella Coola) creation who shaped the world under the direction of the Creator. They made the mountains, rivers, and forests, fashioned the first creatures, and established the pattern of the land that the Nuxalk people know.
source: Nuxalk (Bella Coola) oral tradition; nuxalk.net; Boas Bella Coola texts
research_notes: Attested. The Masmasalanicw are the Four Supernatural Carpenters of Bella Coola creation myth who helped the Creator shape the world and made the first creatures, including the origin of birds. Documented in Boas's Bella Coola texts and Nuxalk tradition (nuxalk.net).

description: Raven, called Qwaxw in Nuxalk, is the culture hero of Bella Coola mythology, a revered transformer who shaped the world for the people. Benevolent in his great acts, he is also a trickster, and many Nuxalk stories tell of his frivolous, ill-considered behavior landing him in trouble.
source: native-languages.org Nuxalk legends; Nuxalk oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Raven (Qwaxw) is the Nuxalk/Bella Coola culture hero and transformer who helps the people, while also a trickster whose careless acts cause trouble. Documented at native-languages.org Nuxalk legends index and in Boas's Bella Coola texts.

description: Coyote, called Talapus by the Chinook, is a trickster of the lower Columbia River peoples, the same comic and creative figure known across the Plateau. Some Chinook tales are told with either Blue Jay or Coyote in the leading role, and Coyote's stories explain landmarks and teach lessons through his blunders.
source: native-languages.org Chinook legends (Talapus); Boas, Chinook Texts
research_notes: Attested. Coyote (Talapus) is a Chinook trickster, often interchangeable with Blue Jay in Chinook tales; the figure derives from Interior Salish and Plateau Coyote traditions absorbed through trade. Documented at native-languages.org and in Boas's Chinook Texts (myth 6 'Coyote').

description: Davy Crockett (1786-1836) is an American frontier folk hero whose real career as hunter, congressman, and defender of the Alamo was stretched by tall tales into legend. In frontier humor he outruns the sun and conquers foes with a grin, and he is a figure of Euro-American, not Native American, folklore.
source: American tall-tale tradition; Britannica 'Davy Crockett'; Lofaro, Davy Crockett
research_notes: Misattributed mythology label. Davy Crockett is a Euro-American frontier tall-tale hero, not an Indigenous North American figure; the input's 'mythology: Indigenous North American' is incorrect and should read American folklore. His legend is documented in tall-tale literature (Lofaro; Britannica). Description corrects the attribution.

The name 'Tihtipihin' could not be verified in the Nuu-chah-nulth sources consulted; the input ties it to Kwatyat, the well-documented Nuu-chah-nulth transformer (Sapir & Swadesh, Nootka Texts), as a brother who helps rescue their mother. Marked unattested pending confirmation of the name and tale.

description: Not independently attested as a distinct named spirit in Chinook folklore. Beaver appears within broader Pacific Northwest animal tales and, most prominently, in the Salish and Kootenai story 'Beaver Steals Fire,' in which Beaver dives to bring fire to the people; a Chinook-specific beaver figure needs better documentation.
source: Johnny Arlee, Beaver Steals Fire (Salish/Kootenai); Boas, Chinook Texts
research_notes: Unattested for Chinook specifically. No named beaver being is recorded for the Chinook in Boas's Chinook Texts. The best-documented beaver figure is 'Beaver Steals Fire,' a Salish and Kootenai legend (Johnny Arlee). Marked unattested with the Salish/Kootenai Beaver as the closest analogue.

description: Komokwa (Kumugwe) is the Undersea Chief of the Kwakwaka'wakw, ruler of the ocean world and giver of wealth. He lives in a copper house beneath the sea filled with treasures, owns the salmon and sea mammals, and is the maker of coppers, the most valued wealth of the potlatch; many families trace their riches to him.
source: Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology (Kumugwe); spiritsofthewestcoast.com; Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Komokwa (Kumugwe) is the Kwakwaka'wakw Undersea Chief, god of tides and maker of coppers, who dwells in a copper house and bestows wealth on families. Confirmed in Wikipedia's Kwakwaka'wakw mythology (citing Boas) and spiritsofthewestcoast.com. The name is Kwakwaka'wakw; the Haida do not call him Komokwa.

description: Huxhukw is the supernatural crane-like cannibal bird of the Kwakwaka'wakw Hamatsa ceremony, a long-beaked attendant of the Man-Eater spirit. It cracks open the skulls of men to suck out their brains, and its masked dancer joins the crooked-beak and raven cannibal birds in the winter dance of the Cannibal Society.
source: Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology; U'mista Cultural Society (Hamatsa)
research_notes: Attested. Huxhukw is one of the supernatural man-eating birds of the Kwakwaka'wakw Hamatsa, a crane-like being that cracks men's skulls to eat their brains. Confirmed in Wikipedia's Kwakwaka'wakw mythology (citing U'mista) and the U'mista Hamat'sa materials.

description: Txamsem, also called Weeget, is the great raven of the Coast Tsimshian, the creator and trickster who stole the sun and stars to light the world and brought fresh water and the salmon. A being of immense appetite and endless ingenuity, he both made the world and causes its troubles, and his deeds are told in Tsimshian adaawx.
source: Wikipedia Tsimshian mythology; Boas, Tsimshian Mythology (1916)
research_notes: Attested. Txamsem/Weeget is the Tsimshian Raven, creator and trickster who brought light, fresh water, and salmon. The Coast Tsimshian call him Txamsem and his brother is Logobola (who caused lack of fresh water and fog); his deeds are told in adaawx origin stories. Documented in Boas's Tsimshian Mythology.

description: Kwatyat is the transformer and culture hero of the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka), who traveled the coast in the myth age setting the world right. He changed the ancient beings into the animals, plants, and landmarks of today, and his journeys, recorded by Sapir and Swadesh, explain the shape of the Nuu-chah-nulth world.
source: Sapir & Swadesh, Nootka Texts; native-languages.org Nootka legends
research_notes: Attested. Kwatyat is the Nuu-chah-nulth transformer/culture hero who reshaped beings and landscape in the myth age, akin to the Transformer figures of other Northwest Coast cultures. Documented in Sapir & Swadesh's Nootka Texts and Nuu-chah-nulth oral tradition.

Coast Salish peoples hold documented beliefs in the land of the dead and in soul-loss, and heroes of the myth age visit the spirit world, but the specific name Tqultca requires better sourcing before it can be verified.

Coast Salish afterlife and soul-loss beliefs are documented (e.g., Adamson 1934; soul-catcher traditions), but the specific term needs confirmation. Marked unattested with the documented spirit-world tradition as the closest analogue.

description: Gwaxwgwakwalanuksiwe' is the man-eating raven of the Kwakwaka'wakw Hamatsa, the most prestigious role among the supernatural man-eating birds that serve the Man-Eater at the North End of the World. As a servant of the cannibal spirit, his masked dance holds the highest station of the Cannibal Society's winter ceremony.
source: Wikipedia Kwakwaka'wakw mythology; U'mista Cultural Society ('Hi'hamsiwe' Hamatsa Supernatural Man-Eater Birds')
research_notes: Attested. Gwaxwgwakwalanuksiwe' is described as the most prestigious role in the Kwakwaka'wakw Supernatural Man-Eater Birds ceremony, a man-eating raven among the servants of Baxbaxwalanuksiwe'. Confirmed via Wikipedia's Kwakwaka'wakw mythology citing U'mista Cultural Society.

description: Evening Star is the celestial daughter of the Sun in the Tsimshian myth of Asdiwal. Appearing on earth as a white bear pursued by the hunter Asdiwal, she carries him into the sky, where he wins her through impossible trials; their union and Asdiwal's later boastfulness are central to the story analyzed by Levi-Strauss.
source: Boas, Tsimshian Mythology (1916); Levi-Strauss, 'The Story of Asdiwal' (1958)
research_notes: Attested. In the Tsimshian Asdiwal myth, the she-bear Asdiwal chases reveals herself as the daughter of the Sun (Evening Star); he wins her through trials. Recorded by Boas (Tsimshian Mythology) and analyzed by Levi-Strauss in 'The Story of Asdiwal.' Four versions were collected between 1895 and 1916.

description: Weeget is the Raven of the Coast Tsimshian, the trickster and creator whose clever thefts gave the people light, fresh water, and salmon. He shapeshifts freely and meddles in the affairs of gods and men, and Tsimshian tellers recount both his world-making deeds and the greed that drives his schemes.
source: Wikipedia Tsimshian mythology; Boas, Tsimshian Mythology
research_notes: Attested. Weeget is the Tsimshian Raven trickster-creator who brought light, water, and salmon through theft and transformation. Same figure as Txamsem; names vary by Tsimshian dialect. Documented in Boas's Tsimshian Mythology and Wikipedia's Tsimshian mythology. Slugs 26, 31, and 35 in this batch are variants of the same Raven figure.

description: Raven is the transformative trickster of Coast Salish peoples, a shapeshifting creator-being who brought light, fire, and salmon into the world. His stories are told from the Squamish to the Halkomelem and Nooksack, where he shares the stage with other animal transformers in the tales of the myth age.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; native-languages.org; Squamish/Halkomelem story collections
research_notes: Attested. Raven is the trickster-creator of the Coast Salish, bringing light, fire, and salmon; he appears across Squamish, Halkomelem, and other Coast Salish traditions. Documented in native-languages.org and regional story collections. The input's story reference is to a transformer tale ('The Two Men Who Changed Things').

description: The Headless Horseman is the ghostly Hessian soldier of Washington Irving's 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' (1820), a figure of Dutch-American folklore of the Hudson Valley. He rides at night with his head carried on his saddle, hurling it at the fleeing Ichabod Crane; he is a classic of American, not Native American, literature.
source: Washington Irving, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (1820); Hudson Valley Dutch folklore
research_notes: Misattributed mythology label. The Headless Horseman is from Washington Irving's 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' (1820), rooted in Dutch colonial folklore of the Hudson Valley, not Native American mythology; the input's 'mythology: Indigenous North American' and 'archetype: guardian' are incorrect. Description corrects the attribution.

description: Ista is the First Woman of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola) origin account, who descended to the land at the beginning of the world and became mother of the people. Her story, told as a smayusta, explains the beginnings of human life and of Nuxalk society and belongs to the creation narratives of the Bella Coola.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; nuxalk.net (smayusta origin stories)
research_notes: Attested. Ista is the First Woman in Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, who descended to the land at Nuxalknalus and became the ancestress of the people; her account is a smayusta (origin story) documented at nuxalk.net. The input's 'demonic-entity' archetype is incorrect; she is a creation ancestress.

He steals the sun to light the world, releases the first salmon, and orders the tides and seasons, while his greed and mischief teach the lessons of the adaawx.
source: Wikipedia Tsimshian mythology; Boas, Tsimshian Mythology
